sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Combat Lifesaver Assistance for Nerve Agent Poisoning
sections.body:
19-50. The CLS must check to verify if the individual has received three sets of ATNAAs. If not, the CLS performs first aid as described for buddy aid above. If the individual has received the three sets of, ATNAA, the CLS may administer additional injections at approximately 15-minute intervals until atropinization is achieved (that is a heart rate above 90 beats per minute, reduced bronchial secretions, and reduced salivations). Administer additional atropines at intervals of 30 minutes to four hours to maintain atropinization or until the casualty is placed under the care of medical personnel. Check the heart rate by lifting the casualty’s mask hood and feeling for a pulse at the carotid artery. Request medical assistance as soon as the tactical situation permits.

19-51. The CLS should administer additional CANA or AAS to casualties suffering from convulsions.

Administer a second, and if needed, a third CANA or AAS at 5-to-10-minute intervals for a maximum of three injections (30mg diazepam or 30mg midazolam). Follow the steps and procedures described in paragraph 19-49 on page 201 for administering the CANA or AAS. DO NOT give more than two additional injections for a total of three (one self-aid plus two by the CLS).

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: BLISTER AGENTS
sections.body: 19-52. Blister agents (vesicants) include mustard, nitrogen mustards, lewisite, and other arsenicals, mixtures of mustards and arsenicals, and phosgene oxime. Blister agents may act on the eyes, mucous membranes, lungs, and skin. They burn and blister the skin or any other body parts they contact. Even relatively low doses may cause serious injury. Blister agents damage the respiratory tract (nose, sinuses, and windpipe) when inhaled and cause vomiting and diarrhea when absorbed. Lewisite and phosgene oxime cause immediate pain on contact. However, mustard agents are deceptive as there is little or no pain at the time of exposure. In some cases, signs of injury may not appear for several hours after exposure.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Protective Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
sections.body:
19-53. Your protective mask with hood and protective over garment provides protection against blister agents. If it is known or suspected that blister agents are being used, STOP BREATHING, put on your mask and your protective over garment.

**CAUTION:** Large drops of liquid vesicants on the protective over garment ensemble may penetrate it if allowed to stand for an extended period.

Remove large drops as soon as possible.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Signs and Symptoms of Blister Agent Poisoning
sections.body:
19-54. Immediate and intense pain upon contact with L, LH (lewisite and mustard) mixture, and phosgene oxime. No initial pain upon contact with mustard.

19-55. Inflammation and blisters (burns) resulting in tissue destruction. The severity of a chemical burn is directly related to the concentration of the agent and the duration of contact with the skin. The longer the agent is in contact with the tissue, the more serious the injury will be.

19-56. Vomiting and diarrhea. Exposure to high concentrations of vesicants may cause vomiting or diarrhea.

19-57. The blister agent vapors absorbed during ordinary field exposure will probably not cause enough internal body (systemic) damage to result in death. However, death may occur from prolonged exposure to high concentrations of vapor or from extensive liquid contamination over wide areas of the skin, particularly when decontamination is neglected or delayed.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: First Aid Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
sections.body:
19-58. Use your RSDL to decontaminate your skin and use water to flush contaminated eyes.

Decontamination of vesicants must be done immediately (within one minute is best).

19-59. If blisters form, cover them loosely with a field dressing and secure the dressing.

**CAUTION:** Blisters are burns. DO NOT attempt to decontaminate the skin where blisters have formed, as the agent has already been absorbed.

19-60. If you receive blisters over a wide area of the body, you are considered seriously burned. Seek medical assistance immediately.

19-61. If vomiting occurs, the mask should be lifted momentarily and drained. Make sure, while doing this, the eyes are closed, and the breath is held. As soon as it is complete, replace, clear, and seal the mask.

19-62. Remember, if vomiting or diarrhea occurs after having been exposed to blister agents, seek medical assistance immediately.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: CHOKING AGENTS (LUNG-DAMAGING AGENTS)
sections.body: 19-63. Chemical agents that attack lung tissue, primarily causing fluid buildup (pulmonary edema), are classified as choking agents (lung-damaging agents). This group includes phosgene, diphosgene (known as DP), chlorine (known as Cl), and chloropicrin (known as PS). Of these four agents, phosgene is the most dangerous and is more likely to be employed by the enemy in future conflict. Your protective mask gives adequate protection against choking agents.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Signs and Symptoms for Choking Agents
sections.body:
19-64. During and immediately after exposure to choking agents (depending on agent concentration and length of exposure), you may experience some or all the following signs and symptoms:

Tears (lacrimation).

Coughing.

Choking.

Tightness of chest.

- Nausea and vomiting.

- Headaches.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Self-Aid for Choking Agents
sections.body:
19-65. The protective mask should be put on immediately when any of the conditions described above exist.

Another indication of a phosgene attack is an odor like newly mown hay; however, DO NOT rely upon odor as indication of a chemical attack.

19-66. If some phosgene is inhaled, normal combat duties should be continued unless there is difficulty in breathing, nausea, vomiting, or more than the usual shortness of breath during exertion. If any of the above symptoms occur and the mission permits, remain at quiet rest until MEDEVAC is accomplished.

**First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Death from Choking Agents**

19-67. With ordinary field exposure to choking agents, death will probably not occur. However, prolonged exposure to high concentrations of the vapor and neglect, or delay in masking can be fatal.

**First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Cyanogen (Blood) Agents**

19-68. Cyanogen agents interfere with proper oxygen utilization in the body. Hydrogen cyanide (AC) and cyanogen chloride are the primary agents in this group.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Protective Measures for Cyanogen Agents
sections.body: 19-69. The protective mask with a fresh filter gives adequate protection against field concentrations of cyanogen agent vapor. Protective over garments, as well as the mask, are needed when exposed to liquid AC hydrogen cyanide.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Signs and Symptoms for Cyanogen Agents
sections.body:
19-70. During and immediately after exposure to cyanogen agents (depending on agent concentration and length of exposure), you may experience some or all the following signs and symptoms:

Tearing (lacrimation).

Eye, nose, and throat irritation.

Sudden stimulation of breathing (unable to hold breath).

- Nausea.

- Headache.

- Unconsciousness.

Coughing.

Tightness of chest.

Light-headedness (dizziness).

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: First Aid for Cyanogen Agents
sections.body:
19-71. Hydrogen cyanide. During any chemical attack, if you get a sudden stimulation to breathe or detect an odor like bitter almonds, PUT ON YOUR MASK IMMEDIATELY. Speed is essential since this agent acts so rapidly that within a few seconds its effects will make it impossible for Service members to put on their mask by themselves. Stop breathing until the mask is on. This may be very difficult since the agent strongly stimulates respiration.

19-72. Cyanogen chloride. Put your mask on immediately if you experience any irritation of the eyes, nose, or throat. The nearest Service member should mask Service members who are unable to mask themselves.

**CAUTION:** Before attempting to help anyone else, make sure you appropriately mask yourself first.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Medical Assistance for Cyanogen Agents
sections.body: 19-73. If exposure to blood agents is suspected, immediate medical assistance is needed. Medical assistance for cyanogen agents is crucial because cyanogen is a highly toxic compound that poses significant health risks to humans. Cyanogen is a colorless gas that can be lethal when inhaled or when it encounters the skin or eyes.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: INCAPACITATING AGENTS
sections.body:
19-74. An incapacitating agent is a chemical agent that produces temporary, disabling conditions, which persist for hours to days after exposure. Unlike riot control agents, which usually are momentary or fleeting in action, incapacitating agents have a persistent effect. It is likely that smoke-producing munitions or aerosols will disseminate such agents, thus making breathing their means of entry into the body. The protective mask is, therefore, essential.

19-75. There are no specific first aid measures to relieve the symptoms of incapacitating agents. Supportive first aid and physical restraint may be indicated. If the casualty is stuporous or comatose, be sure that respiration is unobstructed; then turn them on their side in case vomiting should occur. Complete cleansing of the skin with soap and water, this should be done as soon as possible; or RSDL can be used if washing is impossible. Remove weapons and other potentially harmful items from Service members who are suspected of having these symptoms. Harmful items include cigarettes, matches, medications, and small items that might be swallowed accidentally. Delirious (confused) persons have been known to attempt to eat items bearing only a superficial resemblance to food.

19-76. Incapacitating agents (anticholinergic drugs BZ type) may produce alarming dryness and coating of the lips and tongue; however, there is usually no danger of immediate dehydration. Fluids should be given sparingly, if at all, because of the danger of vomiting and because of the likelihood of temporary urinary retention due to paralysis of bladder muscles.

19-77. Immediate and vigorous cooling of the casualties is indicated if the body temperature is elevated and mucous membranes are dry, (as for heatstroke). The casualty can be cooled by spraying them with cool water and fanning; applying alcohol-soaked cloths and air circulation; and providing maximum exposure to air in a shaded area, along with maximum air circulation. Such cases are usually a result of anticholinergic poisoning.

**CAUTION:** DO NOT use ice for cooling the skin.

19-78. Rapid evacuation should be accomplished since medical treatment with the appropriate medication may be lifesaving. Reassurance and a firm, but friendly, attitude by individuals providing first aid will be beneficial if the casualty appears to comprehend what is being said. Conversation is a waste of time if the Service member is incoherent or cannot understand what is being said. In such cases, the less said, the better it is. These casualties will benefit more from prompt and vigorous restraint and evacuation to an MTF.

**First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: INCENDIARIES**

19-79. Incendiaries can be grouped as white phosphorus (WP), thickened gasoline, metal, and oil and metal.

You must learn to protect yourself against these incendiaries.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: White Phosphorus
sections.body:
19-80. WP is primarily used as a smoke-producing agent but also serves an incendiary role for igniting field expedients and combustible materials. The burns caused by WP are typically multiple, deep, and vary in size.

Once WP particles contact the skin or clothing, they will continue to burn until deprived of air, and they tend to adhere to any surface they contact, requiring physical removal.

19-81. In the event that WP particles ignite clothing, it's crucial to remove the contaminated clothing quickly to prevent the WP from burning through to the skin. If WP particles directly strike the skin, the immediate response should be to smother the flames using water, a wet cloth, or mud. It is important to note that since WP is soluble in oil, one should not use grease or oily substances to extinguish the flames as these can exacerbate the burning.

19-82. To prevent further combustion, keep the WP particles covered with wet material to exclude air.

Removal of WP particles from the skin should be done cautiously using a wet cloth to brush them away and a knife, bayonet, stick, or other available tools to pick them out.

19-83. Once immediate first aid measures are taken, it is vital to seek medical assistance as soon as the mission allows us to address any burns or injuries caused by WP exposure properly.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Thickened Fuel Mixtures (Napalm)
sections.body: 19-84. Thickened fuel mixtures (napalm) tend to cling to clothing and body surfaces, thereby producing prolonged exposure and severe burns. The first aid for these burns is the same as for other heat burns. The heat and irritating gases given off by these combustible mixtures may cause lung damage, which must be treated by medical personnel.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Metal Incendiaries
sections.body:
19-85. Metal incendiaries pose special problems. Thermite particles on the skin should be immediately cooled with water and then removed. The first aid for these burns is the same as for other heat burns. Particles of magnesium on the skin burn quickly and deeply. Like other metal incendiaries, they must be removed.

Ordinarily, medical personnel should do the complete removal of these particles as soon as possible.

Immediate medical treatment is required.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Oil and Metal Incendiaries
sections.body: 19-86. Oil and metal incendiaries, upon contact with skin and clothing, produce effects similar to those caused by white phosphorus. These substances can cause severe burns that require immediate and proper first aid attention to prevent further damage and promote healing. For detailed guidance on administering first aid for burns resulting from exposure to incendiaries like oil and metal, see Chapter 12. This chapter provides comprehensive instructions on the steps to take in treating burns, including how to manage the injury before professional medical help is available.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: FIRST AID IN A BIOLOGICAL ENVIRONMENT
sections.body:
19-87. Biological hazards can provide important advantages to adversaries who use them because of factors such as— Clandestine employment.

- Delayed onset of symptoms.

- Detection, identification, and verification difficulties.

- Agent persistence. Communicability.

19-88. Biological attacks can result in combat ineffectiveness by introducing disease-causing organisms such as bacteria or viruses into the force through aerosol release; food and water contamination; vectors such as ticks, fleas, mosquitoes, or body fluids from infected animals or humans. The occurrence of the signs and symptoms from a biological hazard may appear in a few minutes to several hours or days to weeks depending on the biological hazard, the Service member’s susceptibility, and the amount of biological hazard that is inhaled, ingested, or deposited on the skin. Many biological warfare agents present the same signs and symptoms as the flu or common cold such as fever, cough, runny nose, and tiredness.

19-89. First aid or medical treatment is initiated after a disease is identified, depending on the seriousness of the disease. First aid measures are concerned with observable symptoms of the disease such as diarrhea or vomiting. For certain biological warfare hazards, Service members may be directed to take doxycycline or ciprofloxacin from the initial issue medical CBRN defense materiel.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: TOXINS
sections.body: 19-90. Toxins have reportedly been used in past conflicts. Witnesses and survivors have described the employment of the T-2 mycotoxin as toxic rain (or yellow rain) because it was reported to have been released from aircraft as a yellow powder or liquid that covered ground, structures, vegetation, and people.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Signs and Symptoms of Toxin Poisoning
sections.body:
19-91. The occurrence of the symptoms from toxins may appear in a period of a few minutes to several hours depending on the toxin, the Service member’s susceptibility, and the amount of toxin that is inhaled, ingested, or deposited on the skin. Symptoms from toxins usually involve the central nervous system but are often preceded by less prominent symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, stomach irritation, and burning sensation. Typical neurological symptoms often develop rapidly in severe cases; for example, visual disturbances, inability to swallow, speech difficulty, lack of muscle coordination, and sensory abnormalities (numbness of the mouth, throat, or extremities). Yellow rain (mycotoxins) also may have hemorrhagic symptoms, which could include any or all of the following:

- Dizziness.

Severe itching or tingling of the skin.

Formation of multiple, small, or hard blisters.

Coughing up blood.

Shock (which could result in death).

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Self-Aid of Toxin Poisoning
sections.body:
19-92. Upon recognition of an attack employing toxins, you must immediately take the following actions:

Stop breathing, put on your protective mask with hood, and then resume breathing. Next, put on your protective ensemble.

Should itching of the face become severe or unbearable, quickly— Loosen the cap in your canteen or valve on your water source.

Take and hold a deep breath and lift your mask.

- While holding your breath, close your eyes and flush your face with generous amounts of water.

**CAUTION:** DO NOT rub or scratch your eyes. Try not to let the water run onto your clothing or protective over garment.

Put your protective mask back on, seat it properly, clear it, and check it for a seal; then resume breathing.

- Decontaminate your skin by bathing with soap and water as soon as the mission permits.

Change clothing and decontaminate your protective mask using soap and water. Replace the filters if directed.

19-93. If vomiting occurs, the mask should be lifted momentarily and drained. While doing this, keep your eyes closed, and hold your breath. The mask is then replaced, cleared, and sealed.

**First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: Medical Assistance for Toxin Poisoning**

19-94. If you think you might have been exposed to harmful substances, it's important to get medical help right away. Seeing a doctor quickly can ensure you get the care you need.

sections.heading: First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment: FIRST AID IN A RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR ENVIRONMENT
sections.body:
19-95. Three types of injuries may result from nuclear detonation. These are thermal, blast, and radiation injuries. Many times, the casualty will have a combination of these types of injuries. First aid for thermal and blast injuries is provided based on observable injuries, such as burns, hemorrhage, or fractures.

19-96. The signs and symptoms of radiation illness in the initial phase include the rapid onset of nausea, vomiting, and malaise (tiredness) with first aid measures focused on those observable symptoms and decontamination. If radioactive iodine is released, Service members may be directed to take potassium iodide from the initial issue medical CBRN defense materiel. Potassium iodide is only effective if taken within four hours before or after exposure to radiation from a nuclear or radiological incident. For additional information on first aid in a radiological and nuclear environment see paragraph 1-85 on page 16 or refer to DODM 3150.8, JP 3-11, or ATP 4-02.83.

documents.title: Stress and Psychological First Aid (ATP 4-02.11 Ch. 20)

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: OVERVIEW OF COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS CONTROL
sections.body:
**Chapter 20**

**Combat and Operational Stress Control**

20-1. Psychological first aid is just as crucial as physical first aid and is a familiar concept to many. Think back to when a simple comforting gesture from a parent soothed you as a child, or how supportive conversation with a friend helped you navigate through disappointment or grief. These actions are natural responses to emotional distress, similar to how we instinctively want to help someone who is physically hurt.

20-2. Just as we use bandages to cover wounds, we use supportive words and actions to help heal emotional wounds. Psychological first aid involves assisting those who are emotionally distressed, whether due to physical injuries, illness, or overwhelming stress. Signs of emotional distress, like overexcitement, severe fear, excessive worry, deep depression, or anger, can sometimes be less visible than physical injuries but are equally important to address.

20-3. These emotional reactions are indicators that stress is impacting someone's ability to cope effectively.

When these symptoms become more pronounced, the need for psychological support becomes more urgent.

Knowing how to offer this support is essential, as it can significantly aid in someone's recovery process, just as much as treating a physical ailment.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
sections.body: 20-4. You must know how to give psychological first aid to be able to help yourself, your team members, and your unit to keep performing the mission. Psychological first aid measures are simple and easy to understand. Your decision of what to do depends upon your ability to observe the Service member and understand their needs. Making the best use of resources requires ingenuity on your part. A stress reaction resulting in poor judgment can cause injury or even death to yourself or others on the battlefield. It can be even more dangerous if other personnel are affected by the judgment of an emotionally upset Service member. If it is detected early enough, the affected Service member stands a good chance of remaining in their unit as an effective member. If it is not detected early and if the Service member becomes more emotionally upset, they may become a threat to themselves and to others.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: SITUATIONS REQUIRING PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
sections.body:
20-5. Psychological first aid (buddy aid) is most needed at the first sign that a Service member cannot perform the mission because of emotional distress. Stress is inevitable in combat, in hostage and terrorist situations, and in civilian disasters such as floods, hurricanes, or industrial accidents. Most emotional reactions to such situations are temporary, and the Service member can still carry on with encouragement. Painful or disruptive symptoms may last for minutes, hours, or days. However, if the stress symptoms are seriously disabling, they may be psychologically contagious and endanger not only the emotionally upset Service member but also the entire unit.

20-6. Sometimes people continue to function well during a disastrous event, but suffer from emotional scars, which impair their job performance or quality of life later. Painful memories and dreams may recur for months and years and still be considered a normal reaction. However, an individual needs treatment if the memories are so painful that the person must avoid all situations which arouse them, becomes socially withdrawn, show symptoms of anxiety, depression, or substance abuse. Experience with police, firefighters, emergency medical technicians, and others who deal with disasters have proved that the routine application of psychological first aid to all the participants, including those who have functioned well, greatly reduces the likelihood of future serious post-traumatic stress disorder(s).

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: INTERRELATIONSHIP OF PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PHYSICAL FIRST AID
sections.body: 20-7. Psychological first aid should go together with physical first aid. The discovery of a physical injury or cause for an inability to function does not rule out the possibility of a psychological injury (or vice versa). The person suffering from pain, shock, fear of serious injury, or fear of death does not respond well to joking, indifference, or fearful-tearful attention. Fear and anxiety may take as high a toll of on the Service member's strength as does the loss of blood.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: GOALS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
sections.body:
20-8. Psychological First Aid is aimed at supporting Service members in managing immediate stress reactions effectively, ensuring both the well-being of the individual and the operational readiness of the unit.

The primary goals of Psychological First Aid are multifaceted, focusing on immediate mental health support, safety, and a swift return to duty.

20-9. The first and foremost goal of Psychological First Aid is to provide empathetic support to Service members experiencing stress reactions. By offering a supportive presence, responders can help individuals navigate their emotional responses effectively. This involves active listening, acknowledging their feelings without judgment, and providing reassurance. This supportive approach is crucial in helping Service members feel understood and less isolated in their experiences.

20-10. Another critical aim of Psychological First Aid is to prevent and control behaviors that could be harmful to the individual or others. This includes identifying signs of distress that might lead to harmful actions and implementing strategies to mitigate these risks. The ability to intervene early and effectively can prevent the escalation of stress reactions into more serious mental health issues, thereby maintaining the safety and cohesion of the unit.

20-11. Finally, Psychological First Aid seeks to return the Service member to duty as efficiently as possible after addressing their immediate psychological needs. This goal underscores the importance of resilience and rapid recovery within military operations, ensuring that personnel are mentally fit to resume their roles.

Facilitating a quick return to duty not only helps maintain unit effectiveness but also promotes a sense of normalcy and purpose for the individual, which can be therapeutic in overcoming stress reactions.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: RESPECT FOR OTHERS’ FEELINGS
sections.body:
20-12. Accept the Service member you are trying to help without censorship or ridicule. Respect their right to their own feelings. Even though your feelings, beliefs, and behavior are different, do not blame or make light of them for the way they feel or act. Your purpose is to help them in this tough situation, not to be their critic. A person does not want to be upset and worried. When they seek help, they need and expect consideration of their fears, not abrupt dismissal, or ridicule.

20-13. Realize that people are the products of a wide variety of factors. All people do not react the same way to the same situations. Everyone has complex needs and motivations, both conscious and unconscious, that are uniquely their own. Often the one thing that finally causes the person to become overloaded by a stressful situation is not the stressor itself, but some other problem.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: EMOTIONAL AND PHYSICAL DISABILITY
sections.body:
20-14. Accept emotional disability as being just as real as physical disability. If a Service member’s ankle is seriously sprained in a fall, no one expects them to run right away. A Service member’s emotions may be temporarily strained by the overwhelming stress of battle or another traumatic incident. Do not demand that they pull themselves together immediately and carry on without a break. Some individuals can pull themselves together immediately, but others cannot. The Service member whose emotional stability has been disrupted has a disability just as real as the Service member who has sprained their ankle. There is an unfortunate tendency in many people to regard as real only what they can see, such as a wound or bleeding.

Some people tend to assume that damage involving a person’s mind and emotions is just imagined, they are not sick or injured, and that they could overcome their trouble by using their will power.

20-15. The phrases “it is all in your head”, “snap out of it”, and “get control of yourself” are often used by people who believe they are being helpful. These terms are expressions of hostility because they show lack

of understanding. They only emphasize weakness and inadequacy. The above stated phrases are of no use in psychological first aid.

20-16. Every physically injured person has some emotional reaction to the fact that they are injured. It is normal for an injured person to feel upset. The more severe the injury, the more insecure and fearful they become, especially if the injury is to a body part that is highly valued. For example, an injury to the eyes or the genitals, even though relatively minor, is likely to be extremely upsetting. An injury to some other part of the body may be especially disturbing to an individual for their own reason. For example, an injury to the hand may be a terrifying blow to a surgeon, or an injury to the eye of a pilot.

20-17. An injured Service member can sometimes feel less secure, more anxious, and more afraid not only because of what has happened to them but also what they imagine may happen because of their injury. This fear and insecurity may cause them to be irritable, uncooperative, or unreasonable. As you help the Service member, always keep in mind that such behavior has little or nothing to do with you personally. They need your patience, reassurance, encouragement, and support.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS REACTION
sections.body: 20-18. Stress reaction is a temporary emotional disorder or inability to function, experienced by a previously normal Service member as a reaction to the overwhelming or cumulative stress of combat. Stress reaction gets better with reassurance, rest, physical replenishment, and activities that restore confidence. All Service members are likely to feel stressed under conditions of intense or prolonged stress. They may even become stress reaction casualties and are unable to perform their mission for hours or days. Other combat and operational stress reactions may result in negative behavior, but are not termed stress reaction, as they need treatment that is more intensive. These negative combat and operational stress reactions may result in misconduct and stress behaviors such as drug and alcohol abuse, criminal acts, looting, desertion, and self-inflicted wounds. These harmful combat and operational stress reactions can often be prevented by good psychological first aid. Service members who commit misconduct stress behaviors may require disciplinary action rather than medical treatment.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: REACTIONS TO STRESS
sections.body: 20-19. Most Service members react to stressful incidents after the situation has passed. Service members feel some fear. This fear may be greater than they have experienced at any other time, or they may be more aware of their fear. In such a situation, they should not be surprised if they feel shaky or become sweaty, nauseated, or confused. These reactions are normal and are not a cause for concern. However, some reactions, either short- or long-term, will cause problems if left unchecked.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Emotional Reactions
sections.body:
20-20. The most obvious combat and operational stress reaction is inefficient performance. This can be demonstrated by—

Slow thinking (or reaction time).

- Difficulty recognizing priorities and seeing what needs to be done.

- Difficulty getting started.

Indecisiveness and having trouble focusing.

Tendency to do familiar tasks and be preoccupied with familiar details. (This can reach the point in which the person is very passive, sitting or wandering, and not knowing what to do).

20-21. A less common reaction may be uncontrolled emotional outbursts; this can be demonstrated by crying, screaming, or laughing. Some Service members will react in the opposite way. They can show signs of being very withdrawn, silent, and try to isolate themselves from everyone. These Service members should be encouraged to remain with their assigned unit. Uncontrolled reactions may appear by themselves or in any combination. The person may be crying uncontrollably one minute and then laughing the next. In this state, the person is restless and cannot keep still. They may run about, apparently without purpose. Inside, they feel a great rage or fear and their physical acts may show this. In their anger, they may indiscriminately strike out at others.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Loss of Adaptability
sections.body:
20-22. In a desperate attempt to get away from the danger, which has overwhelmed them, a Service member may panic and become confused. Their mental ability may be so impaired they cannot think clearly or even follow simple commands. Their judgment may be faulty, and they may not be aware of their actions, such as standing up in their fighting position during an attack.

20-23. In other cases, overwhelming stress may produce symptoms that are often associated with head injuries. For example, the Service member may appear dazed or be found wandering around aimlessly. They may appear confused and disoriented and may seem to have a complete or partial loss of memory. In such cases, especially when no eyewitnesses can provide evidence that the Service member has NOT suffered a head injury, it is necessary for them to be rapidly evacuated. DO NOT allow the Service members to expose themselves to further personal danger until the cause of the problem has been determined.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Sleep Disturbance and Repetition of Dreams
sections.body:
20-24. A person who has been overwhelmed by stress, often has difficulty sleeping. The Service member may experience nightmares related to the stressors. Remember that nightmares, in themselves, are not considered abnormal when they occur soon after a period of intensive stress. As time passes, the nightmares usually become less frequent and less intense. In extreme cases, a Service member, even when awake, may think repeatedly of the incident, feel as though it is happening again, and act out parts of their stress repeatedly.

20-25. For some individuals, this repetitious re-experiencing of the stressful event may be necessary for eventual recovery; therefore, it should not be discouraged or viewed as abnormal. For the person re-experiencing the event, such reaction may be disruptive. The Service member needs to be encouraged to ventilate about the incident. Ventilation is a technique where the Service member is given the opportunity to talk extensively and often repetitiously about the experience.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Severe Stress or Stress Reaction
sections.body: 20-26. You do not need specialized training to recognize severe stress or stress reaction that will cause problems for the Service member, the unit, or the mission. Reactions that are less severe, however, are more difficult to detect. To determine whether a person needs help, you must observe them to see whether they are doing something meaningful, performing their duties, taking care of themselves, behaving in an unusual fashion, or acting out of character.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: APPLICATION OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
sections.body: 20-27. The emotionally disturbed Service member has built a barrier against fear. They do this for their own protection, although they are probably not aware that they are doing it. If they find that they do not have to be afraid and that there are normal, understandable things about them, they will feel safer in dropping this barrier. Persistent efforts to make them realize that you want to understand them will be reassuring, especially if you remain calm. Nothing can cause an emotionally disturbed person to become even more fearful than feeling that others are afraid of them. Try to remain calm. Familiar things, such as a cup of coffee, the use of their name, attention to a minor wound, being given a simple job to do, or the sight of familiar people and activities, will add to their ability to overcome their fear. They may not respond well if you get excited, angry, or abrupt.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Ventilation
sections.body:
20-28. After the Service member becomes calmer, they are likely to have dreams about the stressful event.

They also may think about it when they are awake or even repeat their personal reaction to the event. One benefit of this natural pattern is that it helps them master the stress by going over it just as one master the initial fear of parachuting from an aircraft by doing it repeatedly. Eventually, it is difficult to remember how frightening the event was initially. In giving first aid to the emotionally disturbed Service members, you should let them follow this natural pattern. Encourage them to talk. Be a good listener. Let them tell you, in their own words, what happened. If home front problems or worries have contributed to stress, it will help them to talk about these problems. Your patient listening will prove to the Service member that you are

interested in them, and by describing their personal problem, they can work at mastering their fear. If they become overwhelmed, suggest a cup of coffee or a break. Whatever you do, assure them that you will listen again as soon as they are ready. Try to help put the Service member's perception of what happened back into realistic perspective; but DO NOT argue about it.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Activity
sections.body:
20-29. A person who is emotionally disturbed as the result of a combat action is a casualty of anxiety and fear. The person may feel as though they are disabled because they have become temporarily overwhelmed by their anxiety. A good way to control fear is through activity. For example, almost all Service members experience a considerable sense of anxiety and fear while they are poised, awaiting the opening of a big offensive; but this is normally relieved, and they feel better once they begin to move into action. They take pride in effective performance and pleasure in knowing that they are a good Service member, perhaps being completely unaware that overcoming their initial fear was their first major accomplishment.

20-30. Useful activity can be very beneficial to Service members who are emotionally disturbed and not physically incapacitated. After you help a Service member get over their initial fear, help them to regain some self-confidence. Help them realize their job continues by finding them something useful to do. Encourage them to be active. Get them to help load trucks, clean up debris, or dig fighting positions. If possible, get them back to their usual duty. Seek out their strong points and help them apply these attributes. Avoid having them just sit around. You may have to provide directions by telling them what to do and where to do it. The instructions should be clear, simple, and should be repeated. A person who has panicked is likely to argue.

Respect their feelings, but point out more immediate, obtainable, and demanding needs. Channel their excessive energy and, above all, DO NOT argue. If you cannot get them to become interested in doing profitable work, it may be necessary to enlist aid in controlling their over-activity before it results in more panic. Prevent the spread of such infectious feelings by restraining and segregating if necessary.

20-31. Involvement in an activity helps the Service member in three ways; they—

Place their thoughts on something more productive.

- Have an outlet for their excessive tensions.

Prove to them that they can do something useful.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Rest
sections.body: 20-32. There are times, particularly in combat, when physical exhaustion is a principal cause for emotional reactions. A unit sleep plan should be established and implemented. When possible, Service members should be given a safe and relatively comfortable area in which to sleep. Examples would be an area away from heavy traffic, noise, congestion, a place that is clean, dry, and protected from environmental conditions. The more uninterrupted sleep a Service member gets the better they will be able to function in the tactical environment.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Hygiene
sections.body: 20-33. Field hygiene is an important ingredient in a Service member's morale. A Service member who is lacking personal hygiene will not function as well as others who have had the opportunity to bathe and put on clean, dry clothing. During combat, unit leaders should stress the importance of personal hygiene. Good personal hygiene not only improves morale, but it is also a preventive measure against disease and disease and nonbattle injury.

sections.heading: Combat and Operational Stress Control: Group Activity
sections.body: 20-34. You have probably already noticed that a person who works, faces danger, and handles serious problems better if they are a member of a closely-knit group. Each Service member in the team supports the other team members. Esprit de corps is built because the Service members have the same interests, goals, and mission. As a result, they are more productive; and are less worried because everyone is involved. This is one of the most effective tools you have in your psychological first aid bag. Getting the Service member back into the team or squad activities will re-establish their sense of belonging and security. This will go far toward making them a useful member of the unit.

20-39. The Acknowledge, Care, and Escort framework underscores the importance of timely intervention and the need to connect distressed Service members with suitable resources. It offers a practical guide for those who may lack extensive mental health training but are committed to assisting their colleagues.

20-40. The Acknowledge, Care, and Escort approach is a preliminary measure and does not substitute for professional mental health evaluation and treatment. Involving mental health professionals is crucial for a comprehensive assessment and care of Service members experiencing COSRs, ensuring they receive the full spectrum of necessary support.

sections.body:
**First Aid Case and Kits, Authorized Medical Allowance List**

**First Aid Case and Kits, Authorized Medical Allowance List: Appendix A**
